property_summary: For all valid inputs that do not revert, C.transfer(...) always returns true; the mutant returns false for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For every admissible call to transfer (sent by the required sender, with non-empty arrays and amounts that pass the overflow check), the reference C.transfer(...) returns true; the mutant returns false for calls that complete, so there exists inputs where the return value differs (mutant returns false) and thus violates the rule.

For every input arrays where _tos.length == 0 the transfer call returns true in both versions, but for any non-empty _tos the reference accepts and returns true while the mutant reverts (or returns false) because it only allows empty arrays — therefore the general rule: transfer(...) returns true for all calls where _tos.length > 0 under the reference, which the mutant violates for some non-empty input.

For any non-empty _tos array the reference C.transfer(...) always completes successfully and returns true; the mutant that requires _tos.length == 0 will fail (not complete) or behave differently for some non-empty arrays.

For every input where the _tos array is empty or non-empty, the reference C.transfer(...) returns true (completes and returns true) whenever called by the designated sender; the mutant that flips the length check changes acceptance for non-empty arrays — some non-empty arrays that the reference accepts cause the mutant to revert, so the property is: for all inputs with msg.sender == the designated address, C.transfer(...) returns true; the mutant fails this for some non-empty _tos arrays.

For any call made by the designated sender, C.transfer(...) never reverts and always returns true when invoked with any admissible _tos and v arrays (with matching lengths and non-empty allowed); the mutant that requires _tos.length == 0 causes at least some non-empty _tos inputs (from the fuzzer) to make behavior differ, so the property is that calling transfer as the designated sender yields a successful completion (ok == true).

For any caller equal to the designated from address and any non-empty _tos array, the reference C.transfer(...) completes (does not revert) and returns true; the mutant that requires _tos.length == 0 will reject (revert) for some such non-empty inputs, so there exists a non-empty _tos that makes the mutant disagree with this universal completion behavior.

Reference C always only accepts transfer calls when msg.sender equals the hardcoded original owner address (0x9797...), so for any inputs a call from that literal succeeds (subject to other checks) while the mutant which checks msg.sender == from can be made to reject by changing the contract's from state (or by calling from an address that differs from the literal), causing different observable result; thus for all inputs a call from the hardcoded owner should succeed on reference but the mutant can fail for some fuzzed caller addresses.

For any calldata (tos, v) and when called by the literal hardcoded owner address, the reference contract always accepts the call (no revert) while the mutant that checks msg.sender == from can reject calls when the stored `from` differs from that literal; thus the property: calling transfer from the literal owner never reverts on the reference but can revert on the mutant for some fuzzed `from` state/configuration created via deploying a helper that changes c.from by interacting with it (we instead exploit that c.from is a public mutable state and leave it different by construction).

For any fuzzed caller and payload, calling transfer(...) from the contract's hardcoded owner address (0x9797055B68C5DadDE6b3c7d5D80C9CFE2eecE6c9) never reverts on the reference C, while the mutant that requires msg.sender == from can revert for some fuzzed 'from' state or caller — so the property: when msg.sender equals the hardcoded owner literal, transfer(...) returns (does not revert) on the reference for all admissible inputs, but the mutant can fail for some fuzzed inputs.

For any admissible inputs, calling transfer(...) from the original hardcoded owner address (0x9797055B68C5DadDE6b3c7d5D80C9CFE2eecE6c9) does not revert on the reference C, while the mutant that requires msg.sender == from can revert when the contract's stored `from` differs — so the reference always succeeds when invoked by the literal owner but the mutant can fail for some fuzzed `from` state/caller combination.

For every input lists (_tos,v) and any caller equal to the original hard-coded owner literal, the reference C.accepts the call (transfer returns / does not revert); the mutant that checks msg.sender==from can revert when the contract's stored `from` has been changed (i.e. when from != hard-coded owner), so calling transfer from the hard-coded owner is always accepted by the reference but can fail on the mutant for some fuzzed values that set c.from to a different address via an adversarial helper interaction.

For every input list of recipients and uint amounts v, the reference contract always calls the external caddress with the amounts scaled by 10^18 (so the encoded last 32-byte word equals v[i]*1e18) whereas the mutant sometimes encodes a different amount (v[i]*1) and thus the observable encoded amount differs for some fuzzed v; we assert the encoded/observed last call amount (read via a helper callee) equals v[i]*1e18 for all inputs — the mutant will violate this for some inputs.

For any admissible lists (_tos, v) the reference contract always forwards each amount encoded in the external call as v[i]*1e18 (scaling by 10^18); the mutant sometimes forwards v[i]*1 (no scaling), so a callee that records the raw calldata will observe amounts that differ from v[i]*1e18 for some fuzzed v inputs.

For every call to transfer(_tos, v), the correct contract always encodes and forwards each amount as v[i]*1e18 in the external low-level call; the mutant sometimes forwards v[i]*1 (no scaling), so a callee that records the calldata will observe a last-32-byte word different from v[i]*1e18 for some fuzzed v inputs.

For every admissible inputs, C always forwards the uint amounts in the low-level calls scaled by 1e18 (each encoded amount equals v[i]*1e18); the mutant sometimes forwards the unscaled v[i], so a helper callee that records the last 32 bytes of calldata will observe a mismatch for some fuzzed v and recipients.

For every admissible inputs, the reference C always encodes and forwards each uint amount in its external low-level call as v[i]*1e18 (scaling by 10^18); the mutant sometimes forwards v[i]*1 (no scaling), so a callee that records the last 32 bytes of calldata will observe a mismatch for some fuzzed v and recipients.

For any non-empty arrays _tos and v of equal length, the reference C always attempts a call to caddress.transferFrom for every index i in 0.._tos.length-1 (so the number of attempted calls equals _tos.length), whereas the mutant that loops to _tos.length-1 will skip the last recipient and thus attempt strictly fewer calls for any length >=2 (the property detects that by observing a public side-effect count via repeated calls to C.transfer with a helper callee that increments a public counter on each call).

For any non-empty arrays of equal length passed to transfer, the correct contract always causes the callee to be invoked exactly _tos.length times (one call per recipient); the mutant that shortens the loop will invoke the callee fewer times for some inputs (length>=2), breaking this invariant.

For any non-empty arrays _tos and v of equal length, C.transfer always results in the callee at caddress having its public callCount incremented exactly _tos.length times (one external call per recipient); the mutant that shortens the loop will invoke the callee fewer times for some inputs (length>=2), violating this rule.

For any non-empty arrays _tos and v of equal length, C.transfer always returns true (does not revert) while the mutant that reduces the loop bound may still return true but will differ in which external calls occurred; therefore the universal rule we assert here is that calling transfer(...) on the reference C always returns true (no revert) for all admissible inputs, and the mutant can be made to revert for some crafted inputs where the shortened loop causes an out-of-bounds access (e.g., when _tos.length == 1 the mutant's loop upper bound _tos.length-1 underflows in older Solidity versions or, more generally, for certain lengths may lead to incorrect behavior), so asserting that transfer(...) does not revert for all fuzzed inputs distinguishes the reference from the buggy version.

For any non-empty arrays _tos and v of equal length, calling transfer(...) on the reference C always invokes the callee at caddress for every index i (so the callee's public counter equals _tos.length after the call); the mutant that shortens the loop will invoke the callee fewer times for some inputs (length>=2), so the callee's counter will be strictly less than _tos.length for some inputs.

For every call to transfer(...) the reference contract requires the _tos array to be non-empty and therefore never returns true without processing at least one target; the mutant removes that guard allowing a zero-length _tos to return true (no calls) — the rule: transfer(...) must revert or perform at least one external call for empty _tos is forbidden, i.e. reference never returns true when _tos.length == 0, but the mutant can.

For all inputs the reference C never returns true when called with an empty _tos array (it requires _tos.length>0), while the mutant that removed that require may return true for _tos of length 0; the test fuzzes the arrays and asserts that calling transfer with the given arrays never returns true when their length is zero (the reference enforces this for all inputs, the mutant violates it for some).

For any inputs, the reference contract always forwards a call with calldata beginning with the transferFrom function selector (so the external call returns success/behaves deterministically when the callee expects that selector); the mutant omits the selector, causing different calldata which can make the external call revert or behave differently for some callee contracts.

For every admissible input where the caller is the authorized sender and lengths match, C always forwards an external call that succeeds when the callee expects a transferFrom selector-prefixed calldata; the mutant (which omits the selector) can cause the external call to fail for some callee contract, so the reference always returns true while the mutant can revert or return false for some inputs.

For any admissible inputs (authorized caller, non-empty _tos, matching lengths, and each v[i] either zero or safe to scale), C's transfer() always returns true (external calls to caddress succeed because calldata uses the transferFrom selector), whereas the mutant that omits the selector can cause the external call to revert for some callee, making transfer() fail or return false; we assert the call succeeds on the reference for all admissible fuzz inputs and let the fuzzer place a malicious callee address to trigger the mutant's failure.

For any caller, recipient array and amounts where caller is the authorized from and arrays are non-empty and lengths match, the reference C always returns true (external calls to caddress succeed) because it forwards calldata starting with transferFrom selector; the mutant that omits the selector can make the external call fail for a callee that expects the selector, so for some adversarial callee address the mutant's transfer may revert/return false while the reference still returns true.

For any caller/address arrays/amounts where msg.sender is the authorized sender and the arrays are non-empty, C.transfer(...) always returns true (external calls to caddress succeed) when routed to a callee that only accepts calldata prefixed by the transferFrom selector; the mutant that omits the selector will cause such a callee to revert for some inputs, so the mutant can make transfer(...) fail while the reference still succeeds.
